metadata.title: Ride-Sharing Marketplace Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how the ride-sharing marketplace would need to change when city conditions, supply models, regulation, passenger responsibility, airport rules, or customer expectations about pricing change.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: A rider enters pickup and destination in an app. The marketplace prices the request, matches it to a nearby individual driver, tracks one trip, charges the rider, and pays that driver.
metadata.residualArchitecture: Instead of assuming one rider, one individual driver, one fixed pricing method, and one ordinary trip flow, the adapted design separates the trip request, service rules, available supply, vehicle and operator, payer, and passenger. Dispatch can combine individual drivers, fleets, taxis, or automated vehicles; each city can apply zone and service rules; pricing can be fixed, dynamic, or negotiated; and one shared trip record supports safety, payment, explanation, and recovery.
metadata.note: The stressors start in the mobility business context. They are not forecasts and do not assign likelihood; each row asks what must remain after the marketplace is pushed into a different operating attractor.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: A citywide transit strike moves a working day's demand onto the road network
stressors.detection: Transit-agency notices, city operations feeds, rider-intent shifts, road-speed changes, venue calendars, and marketplace-zone telemetry.
stressors.attractor: Demand arrives as a city-scale step change while congestion lengthens every trip and prevents supply from circulating; ordinary nearest-driver matching produces unstable ETAs, cancellations, and inequitable service gaps.
stressors.businessReaction: Publish an explicit constrained-service mode, protect critical trip classes, stage and reserve supply, set honest pickup promises, and coordinate incentives and city messaging by zone.
stressors.residue: Represent a market operating state separately from an individual trip. Dispatch, ETA, pricing, reservation, and communications consume a shared versioned policy envelope with zone capacity, service classes, promise rules, and a graceful-degradation mode.

impacts.effect: Dependability must include honest constrained-service promises during citywide disruption, not only smooth everyday matching.
The rider needs to understand whether a time-sensitive trip can still be fulfilled before committing.
Shows a service class, constrained-zone promise, and alternatives before a request enters dispatch.
ETA promise adherence must be segmented by declared operating state and service class.
Needs an explicit constrained-service experience instead of repeatedly moving an apparently precise ETA.
Consumes a market-state policy envelope and protects scarce capacity across zones and trip classes.
Produces promises from degraded circulation and pickup constraints, not only historical route speed.
Turns reservation and staging into general capacity controls usable outside airport flows.
Owns coherent constrained-market behavior across allocation, pricing, and service promises.
Keeps booking promises honest when citywide disruption changes capacity, pickup, and allocation rules together.
Makes citywide surge resilience and transparent constrained-service behavior part of the competitive benchmark.

stressors.name: An autonomous fleet supplies trips without an individual driver account
stressors.detection: Autonomous-vehicle partnership contracts, pilot-market launches, fleet integration tests, regulator permits, and completed driverless trips.
stressors.attractor: The supply-side customer becomes an operator managing vehicles and remote assistance, while the person normally responsible for accepting, navigating, safety, and earnings is absent.
stressors.businessReaction: Onboard the fleet operator, qualify vehicles by capability and jurisdiction, dispatch eligible trips, expose remote-assistance handoffs, and settle with the operator under a distinct liability model.
stressors.residue: Separate supply provider, operator, vehicle, capability, credential, and human role. Dispatch matches trip requirements to a supply capability contract; safety and settlement attach to accountable parties without assuming that every trip has a driver user.

impacts.effect: Fleet control expands from groups of drivers to mixed estates of human-driven and autonomous vehicles.
Daily marketplace operations need capability, remote-assistance, and liability states per vehicle.
Onboarding establishes operator, vehicle, jurisdiction, capability, insurance, and support relationships independently.
Compliance-ready supply must be measured by vehicle capability and operating domain, not only current driver documents.
Driver workflows become one optional supply-control surface alongside fleet and autonomous interfaces.
Models eligibility for accountable providers, operators, vehicles, and people instead of one driver record.
Matches trip requirements to declared and currently available supply capabilities.
Provides a stable trip, state, intervention, and evidence contract for external autonomous operators.
Assigns monitoring, emergency intervention, and incident accountability when no driver is present.
Owns the operator-facing lifecycle and economics for heterogeneous managed supply.
Lets the rider journey consume autonomous supply through the same reliable trip contract used for human-driven supply.
Makes autonomous partnership readiness part of the reference competitive operating model.

stressors.name: Emergency regulation caps fares exactly when demand exceeds supply
stressors.detection: Emergency orders, city and regulator notices, legal review, fare audits, and rider or driver complaints about affected trips.
stressors.attractor: Price can no longer clear the marketplace during its most constrained state, so unbounded first-come matching creates long waits, strategic cancellations, and weak incentives for drivers to enter the zone.
stressors.businessReaction: Honor the cap, allocate scarce capacity transparently, protect essential or reserved trips, and compensate supply through governed guarantees that are not hidden in the rider fare.
stressors.residue: Separate rider price, capacity allocation, and supplier compensation. A versioned market policy selects non-price controls such as queues, reservations, service classes, and supply guarantees, with an explanation and settlement record for each decision.

impacts.effect: Trustworthy earnings require visible guarantee and allocation rules when rider price cannot respond.
Productive work can be offered through governed guarantees rather than opaque surge alone.
Shows the service obligation and guaranteed compensation attached to a constrained zone.
Offer acceptance quality must distinguish capped, guaranteed, queued, and ordinary work.
Explains queues or protected service rather than implying that a capped fare guarantees immediate supply.
Calculates the legal rider price separately from supplier incentives and allocation priority.
Settles supply guarantees against explicit market-policy versions and fulfillment evidence.
Keeps capped rider charges, platform subsidy, and driver compensation as auditable ledger legs.
Owns the boundary between legal price, marketplace allocation, and supply economics.
Protects understandable driver earnings when rider price can no longer be the only balancing mechanism.
Forces an explicit comparison with negotiated-price models when algorithmic price is constrained.

stressors.name: Guardians ask the marketplace to carry unaccompanied teenagers
stressors.detection: Family-account research, guardian support contacts, school and activity travel requests, safety workshops, and unauthorized-account usage patterns.
stressors.attractor: Requester, payer, passenger, consent giver, safety observer, and support contact are different people, and the marketplace assumes a duty of care it does not have for an ordinary adult self-booking.
stressors.businessReaction: Offer an explicitly eligible service with guardian consent, qualified supply, shared trip visibility, controlled communications, escalation, and post-trip evidence.
stressors.residue: Model trip parties and delegated authority independently. A service-policy contract binds passenger eligibility, guardian consent, driver qualification, communication boundaries, monitoring, and incident handling to the trip record.

impacts.effect: Dependability and safety extend to delegated trips where the app user is not the passenger.
Trust becomes a multi-party job shared by passenger and remote guardian.
Provides guardian visibility and controlled contact without exposing private rider or driver details.
Post-incident churn must be segmented for delegated and duty-of-care trips.
Needs guardian booking, passenger handoff, consent, monitoring, and recovery surfaces.
Separates account holder, payer, guardian, beneficiary, and passenger entitlements.
Captures every trip party, delegated authority, and service-policy version as intent.
Applies qualified-supply, monitoring, communication, and escalation controls for the service class.
Owns the duty-of-care policy, evidence standard, and human escalation design.
Extends the end-to-end trip journey to delegated booking, guardian visibility, and age-specific safety controls.
Makes family and teen ride safeguards a concrete competitive benchmark rather than a generic trust claim.

stressors.name: An airport bans ordinary curb pickup and assigns every platform a remote holding queue
stressors.detection: Airport operating directives, geofence changes, permit feeds, ground-transport partner notices, and pickup-location telemetry.
stressors.attractor: A high-value trip can only be fulfilled through constrained zones, eligible supply, staged capacity, and a regulated release sequence rather than direct nearest-driver matching.
stressors.businessReaction: Configure the airport service state, direct riders to valid handoff points, stage eligible vehicles, release them through the queue, and preserve capped or contracted fare rules.
stressors.residue: No new structural change is required: the market-state policy envelope, supply capability model, and non-price allocation controls already express the airport geofence, provider eligibility, holding capacity, queue, promise, and settlement rules.

impacts.effect: The existing constrained-service model can explain and fulfill the regulated pickup journey.
Uses policy-driven handoff points, queue state, and eligible supply without a special trip architecture.
Airport attach can be evaluated alongside promise quality and constrained-capacity fulfillment.
Renders airport instructions from the same service-policy contract used for other constrained zones.
Configures queue and staging rules as a market operating state rather than airport-only code.
Routes both parties to a policy-valid handoff point and incorporates queue release into the promise.
Can launch the new airport rules primarily through configuration, operational testing, and content.
Lets heterogeneous taxi and private-hire supply compete under the same airport capability and queue rules.
Changes reliable urban mobility to include clear guidance and dependable handoff even when ordinary curb pickup is forbidden.
Carries remote pickup instructions, holding-queue state, and regulated release through one coherent trip flow.

stressors.name: Riders in a growth market expect to negotiate the fare with drivers
stressors.detection: Lost-trip interviews, market-entry research, offer abandonment, driver forums, and adoption of negotiated-price competitors.
stressors.attractor: A platform-defined upfront fare is perceived as less trustworthy than a visible counter-offer process, and liquidity migrates to a marketplace where both sides participate in price discovery.
stressors.businessReaction: Test a bounded negotiation service with safety, time, fairness, cancellation, and earnings guardrails while keeping the trip and payment protections intact.
stressors.residue: Represent price formation as a pluggable, auditable protocol. Trip intent declares an allowed mechanism; offers and counter-offers become expiring events; dispatch consumes an agreed price without owning how that price was formed.

impacts.effect: A trustworthy earnings system must explain the economic tradeoff of accepting, rejecting, or countering an offer.
Finding productive work gains a bounded price-negotiation mode in markets where it is a customer expectation.
Makes the pricing protocol and expected negotiation time visible before request.
Conversion must include negotiation completion time, abandonment, and resulting repeat usage.
Needs safe offer comparison and countering without encouraging distracted or discriminatory behavior.
Publishes guardrails and reference ranges while allowing a distinct market price-formation protocol.
Matches only after a compatible or agreed offer exists, without embedding the negotiation state machine.
Owns experimentation and fairness controls for multiple price-formation modes.
Makes bounded offers and counter-offers part of the driver earning journey without weakening trip or payment protections.
Treats negotiated pricing as a product-model alternative to learn from rather than merely a lower-price competitor.
